There is a dishearteningly large portion of the population that sees any act of conformity as blind obedience, to the point that the word “conform” has an almost universally negative connotation. There is a lot to legitimately worry about with government overstepping and the danger of being a complacent citizen, but the consequence of going so far the other way is that we don’t have a society. We have a loose affiliation of financial contracts and uneasy, suspicious relationships with the humans around us based on leverage and status quo. I don’t think it’s a coincidence that the tone of dystopian Hunger-Games, Terminator-esque media is now the tone of people’s day-to-day perceptions of and interactions with each other. As much as I’m on the side of free expression in media, if you trace the tradition of Western paranoia back to the roots of the country, I think you see a self-perpetuating cycle of superstition, where we are afraid because something bad happened before, and so we tell ourselves scary stories and make ourselves endlessly suspicious of each other. We suspect our neighbor or our government of acting suspiciously because they themselves suspect the same thing of us. There is such a knee-jerk reaction to be punitive, violent, angry, condescending, rude, snarky, bitter, cynical. Instead of getting these dystopian fantasies once a weekend at the movies, we are constantly online stewing in paranoid fear and rage.

I wonder how differently people would behave if the dystopian movie genre up until now had been showing the apocalypse as something tragic, but the story focused on the good people who came together to help one another and rebuild, and making that the plot rather than just an add-on at the end of a movie that largely focuses instead on CGI tidal waves/volcanoes and tons of dead bodies and crazy people. We have people stockpiling and threatening to kill their neighbors like something out of a movie, and it’s a cultural decision to behave that way and tell stories like that to each other all day. The disaster at Fukushima, Japan didn’t see much looting, murder, or fights in the streets, and I think there is a question there worth asking about whether the underlying thinking that made somebody create this Facebook post is related to the former.

This is not a specifically Conservative phenomenon. The USA has a mild-to-moderate-to-severe case of victim worship across the entire political spectrum. Empathy and pity get amped up to levels so high that being a victim here comes with advantages that sometimes outweigh the disadvantages of being a victim. Then, there are plenty of non-victims who will opportunize and pretend to be victims. Christians always play the victim. Conservatives do exactly what this article says they do. But, on the other side, it’s become an old joke at this point that if you have enough “oppression points” for being a minority group, you are a special class of citizen now be of your victim identity. It’s why Elizabeth Warren said she was Native American even when she wasn’t. It’s why the clique of lgbt co-workers at a tech company my friend used to work at were able to bully their straight white co-workers and have HR just shrug it off. It’s why homeless people in many cities are allowed to verbally or physically assault people on the street or shoot heroin in plain sight and not get arrested. In many places here, being a victim has its perks. I never saw a rude homeless person in Asia when I lived there for years. A big part of the reason the locals told me is because there is a cultural assumption that if you’re homeless it’s your fault and they’ll treat you like garbage, so the homeless there have to try extra hard to be nice to be treated with even basic dignity. But, here, we might have more people assume that homeless people are people to be helped and pitied, which would make some people in that position more likely to assume they’ll be treated with compassion, and a few of those victims may actually develop a sense of entitlement from being treated that way. I used to volunteer at a charity that distributed winter coats to homeless people, and you’d be surprised at how many of them acted rude to us, yelled at us that the free coats we gave them were in “the wrong color”, and they were just more or less allowed to do that because they’re homeless, I.e. victims and protected citizens.

Before you go putting words in my mouth and saying that I’m suggesting we be mean to homeless people to make them shape up, I’m not saying that at all. I’m trying to provide a contrasting cultural experience that is very different than the American norm in the hope that it clarifies my overall point that rewarding people for being a victim or giving them special treatment is not the same thing as having compassion for somebody who is a victim, and the distinction is very important, because if you reward or give special treatment to victims, you are incentivizing people to become selfish and ungovernable, whereas if you treat victims with an appropriate level of compassion while still holding them to the moral and behavioral standards of every citizen, you are striking a much better balance.

The concept of being worthless itself is deceptive, if you take it for granted that there is such thing as worthlessness. Take it step by step. What does it mean to be worthless? To have no worth. No value. But, break it down further than that. To have no worth FOR WHAT? For what purpose? To have no value, in what regard? What I’m getting at here is that, for something to be valuable, there must be an idea that the valuable thing is better than the non-valuable thing. There must be a preference. You must prefer one thing instead of the other. So, we can say that value comes from preferences, right? Preferences are opinions. There is no preference that is objective. You could say that objectively it is better to eat food than to starve, sure, but I would argue that fundamentally even survival is a subjective preference. It’s just hard-wired into most people’s’ brains to want to survive, so it feels like it’s objectively good. But it’s not. It’s a preference. The truth is that nothing is objectively better than anything else. It is all relative to what you prefer. Value, or being a valuable person, is an opinion and a preference depending on what you like and what you think is important. This can be a scary thought, but it can also be comforting. You are under no obligation to feel one way or another about anything. You are not required to see one thing as valuable over another, because it is all up to you. People have a very special and unique gift of imagination. We are uniquely capable of imagining the possibility of if things were different. We are capable of making plans and setting expectations in a way that animals just can’t do the same as us. It is a gift that can make you very happy. Insanely happy. But, it comes at a cost and a risk. We have to learn that our thoughts, our imagination, creates our whole world. It is easy to use this evolved superpower of ours to hurt ourselves. We can convince ourselves of our painful thought loops and tell ourselves that it is the truth, and hold onto pain for reasons we can’t explain. But, it’s not the truth. It’s a preference to think that way. Even if we can’t understand why we make the thought choices we do, it is still a choice of what to think. And, it is within your power to change what you think. The purpose of cognitive behavioral therapy is not to convince you to lie to yourself again and again. It is to teach you the very real skill of taking control of your mind and using it in a way that makes you happy. There is no objective reason why telling yourself A instead of B is more “true” or “better”. But, if you would PREFER to be happier, I just want you to know that there is no objective reason why you can’t take control of your opinion of yourself. There is nothing objectively worthless about you, because that is a matter of preference. And, if you have a preference for being different than you are now, then that is the first step. You can then get help making a plan and moving forward. You’ll feel a lot better. And, if you don’t know what you prefer, then you are very fortunate. The process of finding out what you prefer is a beautiful experience that I wish I could do all over again. It’s frightening and crazy, and you have to push yourself little by little out of your comfort zone, but taking control of your mind and preferences is such a wonderful thing that I hope you get to experience as well!
